lesson.title: Letting the Highs Through: The RC High-Pass Filter
lesson.summary: An RC high-pass filter takes the same resistor-capacitor pair from the RC circuit and taps the output across the resistor instead of the capacitor, so high frequencies pass freely while low frequencies are attenuated.
lesson.body:
Remember from the RC circuit that a capacitor's opposition to current, its reactance Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C), depends on frequency. At low frequency Xc is large, so the capacitor behaves almost like an open circuit. At high frequency Xc shrinks toward zero, so the capacitor behaves almost like a short. That single fact, combined with where you choose to measure the output voltage, is the entire secret behind every RC filter.

Build the usual series RC circuit: a resistor and capacitor in series across the input signal. If you take the output across the resistor, you get a high-pass filter. At low frequency, almost all of the input voltage drops across the large reactance of the capacitor, leaving very little across R, so the output is small. At high frequency, the capacitor's reactance collapses, most of the input voltage now drops across R, and the output approaches the full input amplitude. Low frequencies are blocked, high frequencies pass. That matches the behavior promised by the general high-pass filter concept, but now you can calculate exactly where the transition happens instead of just sketching an idealized brick-wall response.

The transition point is called the cutoff frequency, and it occurs where the resistor's value equals the capacitor's reactance, R = Xc. Solving 1/(2*pi*fc*C) = R for fc gives the defining formula of every single-pole RC filter: fc = 1/(2*pi*R*C). At this frequency the output amplitude is not zero and not full scale, it is exactly 1/sqrt(2), about 70.7 percent of the input, which corresponds to a drop of 3 decibels. Below fc, the output magnitude falls off at roughly 20 dB per decade (a factor of ten in amplitude for every hundredfold drop in frequency), which is the same rolloff rate you would find in a low-pass filter, just mirrored to the other side of fc.

Try it with real numbers. Let R = 1 kilohm and C = 0.1 microfarads (1.0 x 10^-7 F). The time constant product is RC = 1000 x 1.0e-7 = 1.0 x 10^-4 seconds, so fc = 1/(2*pi*1.0e-4) = 1/(6.283 x 10^-4) which works out to about 1591.5 Hz. Now ask what happens well below that cutoff, say at f = 100 Hz, with a 5 V input amplitude. The angular frequency is w = 2*pi*100 = 628.3 rad/s, so wRC = 628.3 x 1.0e-4 = 0.06283. The high-pass magnitude ratio is wRC / sqrt(1 + (wRC)^2) = 0.06283 / sqrt(1.00395) = 0.06283 / 1.00197, which comes out to about 0.0627. Multiply by the 5 V input and the output is only about 0.31 V, roughly 24 dB down. Check that against the rolloff rule: 100 Hz is about 1.2 decades below the 1591.5 Hz cutoff, and 1.2 decades times 20 dB per decade is 24 dB, which matches the direct calculation almost exactly. That agreement is a good habit to build: whenever you compute a filter's response at a specific frequency, sanity check it against the simple decade-based rolloff rule.

This same resistor-capacitor pair, wired the other way with the output across the capacitor instead of the resistor, is the RC low-pass filter you have already met. Nothing about the components changed, only where you chose to read the output. Keep that lesson in mind, because the same trick, swapping which element the output is measured across, is exactly how the next two filters in this chapter turn a single RL circuit into either a low-pass or a high-pass response.
